name: compare-prose

density.note: each side's case in a sentence or two

split.note: FIDELITY: cover (the question) → one subject per page → verdict, on the shared cover finish (was editorial). lib/core/carousel.js.

description: Two prose options side-by-side with a labeled corner tag on each.
purpose: Use to weigh two approaches against each other in body text. Add the `chosen` or `decision` modifier to mark the verdict; add `vertical` to stack top/bottom instead of side-by-side. `axis` reframes the pair as two facets of one idea — a lede above, a numeral-led card per facet, a closing note below.

options.description: Exactly two list items, each one option. The lead text is the option label — it renders bold automatically (no `**…**` needed); follow it with a nested bullet carrying 1–3 sentences. In `axis`, leave the lead blank and nest a 3-item sub-list instead: the facet numeral (`I` / `II`), a bold title, and a description sentence.

lede.description: `axis` only. A framing sentence between the heading and the two facet cards.

note.description: A closing line after the two cards. Plain prose in the base layout; `axis` renders it centered and italic.

skeleton:
<!-- _class: compare-prose -->

## Heading framing the comparison.

- First option
  - Two-sentence description of the first option, including the strongest argument for it.
- Second option
  - Two-sentence description of the second option, including the strongest argument for it.
sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose -->

## Two options, equal footing, corner tags.

- The left option
  - Each pane holds one option's case in up to twenty words of prose, tagged at the corner.
- The right option
  - The panes stay symmetric; a longer case belongs in the vertical variant, not a taller card.

stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose vertical -->

## Two full cases is the most this pair holds.

- The stressed top pane
  - A case at the hard budget runs about this long: two full sentences that state the option, its strongest argument, and the cost it accepts — and then stops.
- The stressed bottom pane
  - Symmetry matters most at the ceiling; when one pane runs half the other's length, the slide reads as a verdict the author did not intend to give.

whenToUse.title: Two prose alternatives
whenToUse.body: Both sides are full sentences of argument, not lists of facts. The audience reads each column as a paragraph and weighs them against each other.

whenToUse.title: Equal-density prose
whenToUse.body: Each card carries roughly the same body length. One short and one long breaks the visual symmetry that makes the comparison legible.

whenToUse.title: Add a verdict modifier when chosen
whenToUse.body: Layer `chosen`, `decision`, or `vertical` to name the editorial intent. The default (neutral two-up) reads as still-being-decided.

antiPatterns.title: Code comparison
antiPatterns.body: Use `compare-code` for two fenced blocks. compare-prose is for sentences, not snippets.

antiPatterns.title: Three or more options
antiPatterns.body: compare-prose is strictly two. For three or more, use `cards-grid three` or `verdict-grid` with criteria badges.

antiPatterns.title: Verbatim text differences
antiPatterns.body: When the diff lives inside the prose itself — legal language, contract clauses — use `redline` so insertions and deletions render inline.

related.when: the columns are code, not prose

axis.label: axis
axis.summary: A lede above, numeral-led facet cards, a closing note below.
axis.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose axis -->

## The second axis: how far it reaches.

The verb is one axis — how you think. **Reach** is the other — how far what you make travels.

1. Own the verb
   - You can do the cognitive work — correct, clear, complete. It reaches only you.
2. Widen the reach
   - The work travels: team, org, field. Documented, adopted, durable.

*Most engineers stall on making it travel, not on the thinking.*

transition.label: transition
transition.summary: Left reads as before, right as after.
transition.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose transition -->

## transition reads left as before, right as after.

- Before
  - The arrow between the panes turns comparison into change over time.
- After
  - Use it for state changes, not preferences — the arrow implies causation.

mirror.label: mirror
mirror.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose mirror -->

## mirror swaps the reading order.

- Second option
  - mirror renders this pane first — for when the deck's rhythm lands on the left.
- First option
  - Same anatomy, flipped; the corner tags travel with their panes.

chosen.label: chosen
chosen.summary: Crowns the right pane the winner.
chosen.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose chosen -->

## chosen crowns the right pane the winner.

- The road not taken
  - The losing option keeps its full case — an honest comparison shows real strength.
- The verdict
  - The accent treatment marks this pane as the pick; pair with a reason, not a repeat.

decision.label: decision
decision.summary: Stamps the verdict banner across the pair.
decision.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose decision -->

## decision stamps the verdict banner across the pair.

- Option one
  - Both panes stay equal; the banner above carries the call.
- Option two
  - Use when the decision is made and the slide is the record.

vertical.label: vertical
vertical.summary: Stacks the panes for longer cases.
vertical.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose vertical -->

## vertical stacks the panes for longer cases.

- The top option
  - Stacking buys full slide width, so a case may run toward its ceiling without the columns pinching.
- The bottom option
  - The trade is simultaneity — the eye compares in sequence, so lead with the keeper.

banner-tag.label: banner-tag
banner-tag.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose banner-tag -->

## banner-tag fills the corner tags at banner weight.

- OPTION A
  - The tag takes the accent fill and full contrast.
- OPTION B
  - Use for short, loud labels — verdicts, camps, teams.

rejected.label: Rejected
rejected.sample:
<!-- _class: compare-prose rejected -->

## rejected strikes the losing pane.

- The pick
  - The surviving option reads at full strength.
- The rejected pane
  - Dimmed and struck — the record of what was considered and declined.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming `chosen`/`rejected`/`decision` mark whichever option is authored first.
commonMistakes.fix: All three target the SECOND card (`li:last-child`) in the markdown — the option to crown (`chosen`) or strike (`rejected`) must be written second, not first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Combining `mirror` with `chosen`/`rejected`/`decision`, expecting the marked card to move with the visual swap.
commonMistakes.fix: `mirror` only reverses the VISUAL row (`flex-direction: row-reverse`) — the chosen/rejected treatment still targets the second option in markdown SOURCE order, so mirroring changes where it appears on screen, not which option gets the accent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a label before the nested sub-list in an `axis` card (`- Own the verb` then the numeral/title/description sub-list), the way the base layout's option lead works.
commonMistakes.fix: `axis` cards read the FIRST three items of the nested sub-list as numeral, title, and description — leave the outer bullet's own lead blank (`- ` with nothing after it) so nothing is left over to become a stray corner tag.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: Two FACETS of one idea, not a before/after change of state — authored as a numbered list (`1. Title` + a nested body line). The I/II numerals are generated from the ol counter, never typed, and the variant opts out of the family's corner-tag treatment so the title stacks under the numeral.
The comparison is a state change over time — left is before, right is after; implies causation, not two co-equal preferences.
Same anatomy, but the deck's rhythm wants the accented (second) option to land visually on the left instead of the right.
One option is the winner and the other keeps its full, undiminished case — crowns the second option without dimming the first.
The decision is made and the slide is the record — composes `chosen` with a de-emphasized first card and a stronger connector.
Either case needs more room than the two-column width can hold — stacks the panes top/bottom instead of side by side.
The corner labels are short, loud verdicts (camps, teams) that deserve a full-width banner instead of a quiet corner tag.
One option was considered and explicitly declined — dims and strikes the second card as the record of what didn't make it.
